in.other_title: No PGR or SGR analogue because easy-only training can beat full training
in.rationale: Hase et al. define Supervision Gap Recovered with hard-data finetuning as the 100% reference. Sun et al. decline to define an SGR or PGR analogue because models trained only on easier tasks, particularly with RL, sometimes outperform those trained on all levels, which would push such metrics above 100%; Sun et al. report generator performance on the MATH500 test set, with generators optionally optimised by the evaluator, while Hase et al. compare finetuning on easy, hard or no data (zero-shot).
in.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: whether a gap-recovered metric with a hard-data oracle as upper bound is suitable for easy-to-hard evaluation

open_obligations: Check that Hase et al.'s SGR uses training on hard data as the ceiling, so that exceeding it would break the metric
Check how often easy-only training actually exceeds full training in Sun et al.'s tables

Sun et al. compare easy-only training, particularly with RL, against training across all difficulty levels, not against Hase et al.'s finetuning on hard data, so their observation does not directly show easy-only training exceeding SGR's Hard term
in.other_title: Sun et al. decline Hase et al.'s SGR metric because easy-only training can beat full training
in.rationale: The authors choose not to establish an SGR-style metric because models trained only on simpler tasks, particularly with RL training, can outperform those trained across the entire spectrum of problem difficulties, which shows a limit of the metric's applicability in their setting without a direct conflict with Hase et al.'s findings, so CHALLENGES. Hase et al.'s SGR compares finetuning on easy data, hard data, or no data (zero-shot).
in.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: Whether a supervision-gap-recovered metric anchored on hard-data training is meaningful; holds where easy-only training can outperform training across the entire spectrum of problem difficulties

text: The authors define Supervision Gap Recovered as (Easy - Unsupervised) / (Hard - Unsupervised), where Easy, Hard and Unsupervised are hard-test performance after finetuning on easy data, on hard data, or on no data (zero-shot). SGR is 100% when easy data is as effective as hard data and 0% when the easy-finetuned model is no better than zero-shot prompting.
title: Supervision Gap Recovered (SGR) metric for easy-to-hard generalization
